scenario: AITA for not buying my siblings gifts because they refuse to do a secret Santa? | I have a bunch of siblings, all grown adults, and buying gifts for everyone including parents, partners, and kids is out of control. While I am financially okish, I just can't afford it. Also, neither can my parents and previous years have resulted in my mom being depressed and stressed trying to buy everyone something. Last year, after a some resistance, we agreed to do a secret santa and it went pretty well. Or so I thought. This year 1 sibling threw a fit about doing it. She said she doesn't like "putting rules on holidays" and it's not fair. As a side note, she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything. Last year was the 1st time everyone brought something. Another sibling, who is hosting Christmas, sided with her and said that we won't do a secret Santa but that you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. Am an asshole if I don't buy my siblings gifts? I love my family but I can't afford it this year. I was going to get nieces and nephews gifts but that's it.

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's see. The user is a man asking if he's an asshole for not buying his siblings gifts because they refused to do a secret Santa. He's explaining that he can't afford to buy gifts for everyone, including parents, partners, and kids. Previous years caused his mom stress and depression. Last year they did a secret Santa which worked, but this year one sibling is against it, saying it's putting rules on holidays and unfair. Another sibling, the host, says they won't do secret Santa but you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. He wants to know if he's wrong for not buying gifts for siblings, only getting gifts for nieces and nephews.

First, I need to evaluate the moral acceptability of his action. The key points here are financial constraints, previous stress on the family, and the fact that the siblings themselves are not participating in gift-giving. The user is saying he can't afford it, and his mom was stressed before. Last year's secret Santa was a solution that worked, but this year some siblings are refusing to participate. The host sibling says you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. So the user is considering only buying for the kids (nieces/nephews) and not the siblings.

Now, moral acceptability. Is it wrong to not buy gifts for siblings when you can't afford it, especially when others aren't participating either? Let's think about common moral standards. Generally, gift-giving is a voluntary act, especially among adults. There's no strict moral obligation to give gifts unless there's a prior agreement or cultural expectation. However, in family contexts, sometimes there's an expectation, but if the family has agreed to a secret Santa to reduce the burden, and some members are refusing to follow that, then the user's decision to not buy gifts for siblings might be reasonable.

The user mentioned that previous years caused his mom stress, so the secret Santa was a way to alleviate that. Now, one sibling is against it, but the host says you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to. So the family is moving away from the secret Santa, but the user is choosing to only buy for the kids. Since he's financially constrained and the siblings aren't contributing either (as per "she and our younger siblings rarely buy anyone anything"), it's reasonable for him to not buy gifts for them. If others aren't participating, then he's not obligated to bear the cost alone.

Also, the fact that he's still buying for the nieces and nephews shows he's still participating in some way, but not overextending himself. Morally, it's acceptable to set boundaries when you can't afford something, especially when others aren't contributing. There's no moral duty to spend beyond your means, especially when it's causing stress. The siblings who are refusing to do secret Santa are not holding up their part, so the user isn't being unfair by not buying for them.

Another angle: if the family had a prior agreement to do secret Santa, but some are backing out, then the user is within his rights to follow the new agreement (since the host said you don't have to bring gifts if you don't want to). So if the family is now not doing secret Santa and it's optional, then he's choosing not to buy for siblings, which is acceptable.

So the action is morally acceptable. Therefore, answer 1.
